$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={e}^{y}={e}^{4\operatorname{sin}⁡t}, \\ Q(x,y) & ={e}^{x}={e}^{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitutions $u=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t,du=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt$ and $v=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,dv=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,dt,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({e}^{4\operatorname{sin}⁡t})\cdot (4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-({e}^{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t})\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({e}^{4\operatorname{sin}⁡t})\cdot (4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({e}^{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t})\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{0}{e}^{u}\,du-{\int }_{1}^{1}{e}^{v}\,\text{d}v \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-452bd17e-660a-568a-8108-39d6d0770162"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=5\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =x+y=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t+5\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $\operatorname{sin}⁡t=u,du=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t+5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }15{cos}^{2}⁡t+9\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+15{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }15\,\text{d}t+9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }15\,\text{d}t+9{\int }_{0}^{0}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =15t{|}_{0}^{2\pi }+0 \\  & =15(2\pi -0) \\  & =30\pi \end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8411ac91-aa07-508a-9904-aa0a020877bc"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $5$ and $2,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={e}^{y}={e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}, \\ Q(x,y) & ={e}^{x}={e}^{5\operatorname{cos}⁡t}.\end{aligned}

:question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $3$ and $2,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={y}^{2}=4{sin}^{2}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =xy=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(4{sin}^{2}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }8{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+18{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }26{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{1}26{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186177915 :answer-field/correct 17592186177919 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-735394db-bfa6-5cb2-9d7d-19fe3d01e994" :question/id #uuid "735394db-bfa6-5cb2-9d7d-19fe3d01e994" :question/math-academy-id "q-127256" :question/problem "![](images/62/62c8f6d7db345ce76bd164bb52c13e5edef9c04f18f4f07501c8694e7f64b554.png)

The curve $C$ is given by $x={e}^{y}$ from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(e,1).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)={y}^{2}\,i+\frac{1}{x}\,j$ through $C,$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above." :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

Parameterizing the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={e}^{t}\,y=t,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(e,1).$ Therefore, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

![](images/ba/ba6285008fd90835fdbf73203b76a0a01d713889d9939979aaec54bebd0a8c49.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={y}^{2}={t}^{2}, \\ Q(x,y) & =\frac{1}{x}={e}^{-t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})={e}^{t}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2})\cdot (1)-({e}^{-t})\cdot ({e}^{t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}-1\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}-t){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{3}-1)-0 \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

Parameterizing the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y=\frac{1}{t},\,t\in [\frac{1}{2},2].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point $(\frac{1}{2},2)$ to the point $(2,\frac{1}{2}).$ Therefore, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux.

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={x}^{2}y=t, \\ Q(x,y) & =-y=-\frac{1}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})=-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}(t)\cdot (-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})-(-\frac{1}{t})\cdot (1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}0\,\text{d}t \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-5f7eefb0-93b0-549d-9805-f25d2ffc89e0"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-5f7eefb0-93b0-549d-9805-f25d2ffc89e0" :answer-field/id #uuid "5f7eefb0-93b0-549d-9805-f25d2ffc89e0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-0a0fbaf0-fbaf-5ffb-ba78-e300b9c3cb2c" :answer-field/choices ["answer-527da9e8-31b2-5d12-ada1-f6448689e756" "answer-d6be670d-4038-5dbc-ac98-7208e5a8c53f" "answer-0a0fbaf0-fbaf-5ffb-ba78-e300b9c3cb2c" "answer-b79b1436-2e95-5a91-a8c3-0d137af242fb" "answer-dfbe47bf-91a3-5026-b0f2-e265e56e1b7f"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-527da9e8-31b2-5d12-ada1-f6448689e756" :answer/id #uuid "527da9e8-31b2-5d12-ada1-f6448689e756" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d6be670d-4038-5dbc-ac98-7208e5a8c53f" :answer/id #uuid "d6be670d-4038-5dbc-ac98-7208e5a8c53f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0a0fbaf0-fbaf-5ffb-ba78-e300b9c3cb2c" :answer/id #uuid "0a0fbaf0-fbaf-5ffb-ba78-e300b9c3cb2c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b79b1436-2e95-5a91-a8c3-0d137af242fb" :answer/id #uuid "b79b1436-2e95-5a91-a8c3-0d137af242fb" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-dfbe47bf-91a3-5026-b0f2-e265e56e1b7f" :answer/id #uuid "dfbe47bf-91a3-5026-b0f2-e265e56e1b7f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186180728 :tutorial/content "Let's now derive the following formula for the flux:

:question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $3$ and $2,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={y}^{2}=4{sin}^{2}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =xy=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(4{sin}^{2}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }8{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+18{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }26{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{1}26{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186177915 :answer-field/correct 17592186177919 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-735394db-bfa6-5cb2-9d7d-19fe3d01e994" :question/id #uuid "735394db-bfa6-5cb2-9d7d-19fe3d01e994" :question/math-academy-id "q-127256" :question/problem "![](images/62/62c8f6d7db345ce76bd164bb52c13e5edef9c04f18f4f07501c8694e7f64b554.png)

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

Parameterizing the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={e}^{t}\,y=t,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(e,1).$ Therefore, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

![](images/ba/ba6285008fd90835fdbf73203b76a0a01d713889d9939979aaec54bebd0a8c49.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={y}^{2}={t}^{2}, \\ Q(x,y) & =\frac{1}{x}={e}^{-t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})={e}^{t}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2})\cdot (1)-({e}^{-t})\cdot ({e}^{t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}-1\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}-t){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{3}-1)-0 \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-04fdbb04-1f5e-524e-9c27-6e5e40173080"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-04fdbb04-1f5e-524e-9c27-6e5e40173080" :answer-field/id #uuid "04fdbb04-1f5e-524e-9c27-6e5e40173080" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-6097d82c-a160-580e-ba98-359ee8f02940" :answer-field/choices ["answer-5f942441-ff7e-546f-8b6c-c0bc3ed8b008" "answer-6097d82c-a160-580e-ba98-359ee8f02940" "answer-8ebff72e-dab2-5efc-93c1-8a98f5c588a0" "answer-a5ebd4b0-5c2f-5c66-823d-14cb8a9a334c" "answer-54352619-e7d8-51ab-bf81-2466d57fb916"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5f942441-ff7e-546f-8b6c-c0bc3ed8b008" :answer/id #uuid "5f942441-ff7e-546f-8b6c-c0bc3ed8b008" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{1}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6097d82c-a160-580e-ba98-359ee8f02940" :answer/id #uuid "6097d82c-a160-580e-ba98-359ee8f02940" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{2}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8ebff72e-dab2-5efc-93c1-8a98f5c588a0" :answer/id #uuid "8ebff72e-dab2-5efc-93c1-8a98f5c588a0" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a5ebd4b0-5c2f-5c66-823d-14cb8a9a334c" :answer/id #uuid "a5ebd4b0-5c2f-5c66-823d-14cb8a9a334c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-54352619-e7d8-51ab-bf81-2466d57fb916" :answer/id #uuid "54352619-e7d8-51ab-bf81-2466d57fb916" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-ddff35a9-8792-529b-9827-d26481dbe529" :question/id #uuid "ddff35a9-8792-529b-9827-d26481dbe529" :question/math-academy-id "q-127235" :question/problem "![](images/95/95e6a455863f0b4cefe184cca9ad86feaeff9f0702808db2d151f5d6615a04b8.png)

$$

$$

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

Parameterizing the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y=\frac{1}{t},\,t\in [\frac{1}{2},2].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point $(\frac{1}{2},2)$ to the point $(2,\frac{1}{2}).$ Therefore, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

![](images/cc/cc9d66f800a57f27673577cd3fd179b4cd6ff64585c5dc1a867317d8d592e485.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={x}^{2}y=t, \\ Q(x,y) & =-y=-\frac{1}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})=-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}(t)\cdot (-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})-(-\frac{1}{t})\cdot (1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}0\,\text{d}t \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-ddff35a9-8792-529b-9827-d26481dbe529" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-5f7eefb0-93b0-549d-9805-f25d2ffc89e0" :answer-field/id #uuid $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{1^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{3^2} = 1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $1$ and $3,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \cos{t}\,\mathbf{i} +3\sin{t}\,\mathbf{j},
\qquad 0 \leq t \leq 2\pi.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = \cos t, \qquad
y = 3\sin t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =xy=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & ={x}^{2}={cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $u=\cos t, \textrm d u = -\sin t\,\textrm d t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-({cos}^{2}⁡t)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }9\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }10\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{1}^{1}10{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048540} {:db/id 17592186180030 :question/id #uuid "f1687af9-fdc5-568f-9b8e-74b394a32f6f" :question/math-academy-id "q-126719"} {:db/id 17592186180041 :question/id #uuid The curve $C$ is given by $y = \dfrac14x^2$ from the point $\left(0,0\right)$ to the point $\left(4,4\right).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = -2\,\mathbf{i} + x\,\mathbf{j}$ through $C,$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ on $C,$ as shown above." :question/worked-solution "If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $\mathbf r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ *must* be a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $\mathbf T(t).$

Parameterizing the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = t, \qquad
y = \dfrac{t^2}{4},
\qquad
t\in \left[0,4\right].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point $(0,0)$ to the point $(4,4).$ Therefore, $\mathbf n$ is indeed a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation of $\mathbf T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

![](images/2b/2b94e24344f600fc02ec5ecac6c1e0ee4c6a5450132753a0a5ac5fceaa9aa1fc.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =-2, \\ Q(x,y) & =x=t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{t}^{2}}{4})=\frac{t}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}(-2)\cdot (\frac{t}{2})-(t)\cdot (1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}-2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{t}^{2}{|}_{0}^{4} \\  & =-16-0 \\  & =-16\end{aligned}
